rationale: The book's core identification that 'works' are deeds (not synonyms for obedience) is the most precise and best-supported reading of the printed texts. Exodus 18:20 defines work as the concrete deed shown after ordinances and the way to walk; Luke 17:7-10 and Romans 4:4-5 then distinguish the same deed from any wage-claim even when the deed fully obeys; James 2:21-22 shows the identical category of deed making faith visible rather than purchasing standing. The common interpretation correctly notes that works often function as fruit or evidence, yet that is a secondary use that presupposes the prior lexical identification of the deed itself. No stronger counter explains the full set of printed references with fewer unsupported steps.
book_core_identification: Works are deeds/actions; a work becomes obedience only when it executes a legitimate command and becomes disobedience when it conflicts with God's command; works are therefore not a synonym for obedience.
book_secondary_elaborations: Romans 4 frames the laborer's work as a wage-claim that creates debt rather than grace
James 2 frames Abraham's work as faith made visible/perfect
Even complete obedience earns no wage (Luke 17: unprofitable servants who have only done their duty)
Works remain commandment-shaped and can be 'kept' (Revelation 2:26; Psalm 111:7 pairing works and commandments)
Paul's 'works of the law' usage is context-sensitive and never equates every deed with a purchase price
strongest_counter_interpretation: The mainstream Christian reading that 'works' primarily means the outward deeds that express and evidence the inner spiritual condition (good works as fruit of faith/grace, evil works as fruit of the flesh/unbelief), functioning as the visible basis of judgment while remaining distinct from the root of justifying faith.
counter_core_identification: Works are deeds functioning primarily as evidence/fruit of the heart's true spiritual state rather than as the root of standing with God.
material_core_denial: The counter does not deny that works are deeds; it simply embeds the evidential/fruit role as the primary theological definition and does not foreground the book's sharper non-synonymy with obedience or the wage-claim distinction.
counter_case: Ephesians 2:8-10 and Titus 3:5 exclude works as the source of salvation while requiring good works as the created purpose
James 2:14-26 and Matthew 7:16-20 treat works as the evidence that living faith (or a good tree) is present
Revelation 20:12-13 and Romans 2:6 make works the criterion of judgment precisely because they manifest the heart
Galatians 5:19-23 contrasts works of the flesh with fruit of the Spirit, reinforcing the evidence reading
book_explanatory_advantages: Directly accounts for Exodus 18:20's sequential definition (ordinances taught, way walked, work done) without collapsing work into obedience
Preserves the economic picture of Romans 4:4-5 (work offered for debt/wages) while still allowing James 2's non-meritorious visibility of faith
Explains Luke 17:7-10's 'unprofitable servants' who have done every commanded thing yet claim no wage, which pure fruit-language leaves under-specified
Keeps the lexical category of deed stable across good works, evil works, and 'works of the law' without requiring a different referent for each context
counter_explanatory_advantages: Matches the dominant pastoral and confessional emphasis that good works are necessary fruit rather than meritorious cause
Integrates the judgment texts (Rev 20, Rom 2) and the tree-fruit imagery (Matt 7) under a single functional description
Handles the soteriological tension between Paul and James without inventing new lexical senses
unresolved_objections: The book does not fully systematize every New Testament occurrence of 'works of the law' or Johannine 'works' of Jesus within the printed entry itself (those are deferred to the larger chapter)
Catholic/Orthodox cooperative-meritorious readings remain possible once the core deed identification is granted; the entry does not adjudicate final soteriology
